evidence_quotes.quote: We study water demand among non-tap households in three cities in El Salvador and in marginal barrios in Tegucigalpa, Honduras, using data from identical household studies in the four cities.
Our utilized data set covers water consumption and related costs for 553 non-tap households in El Salvador and 826 non-tap households in Honduras.

In order to avoid ad hoc speciﬁcations of these functions, we propose to estimate a reduced-form model where households’ choice of each speciﬁed water source is written as a function of households’ characteristics.

We include as explanatory variables household monthly income (in USD, PPP corrected), lot size (in square meters), constructed area (in square meters), number of persons in residence, number of children less than 5 years old, and dummies for electricity availability, and whether the respondent reads and writes.
In what follows, demand is deﬁned as total water consumption (including free water) per capita per month (measured in cubic meters).

As our primary interest is to compare elasticities of demand with respect to total water cost (hauling cost plus price of water) across coping sources, we allow the parameters of the cost variable to vary across sources.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household non-tap ('coping') drinking/domestic water source selection and water consumption among unconnected urban households in three cities in El Salvador and marginal barrios in Tegucigalpa, Honduras.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, the study does not empirically examine any legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor: while Section 3.1.1 briefly notes in theory that municipal authorities may locate public taps or truck routes and mentions descriptively that the Tegucigalpa sample comes from marginal barrios (unincorporated squatter communities), the authors explicitly avoid modeling municipal or institutional supply decisions and instead estimate a reduced-form household model using only household socioeconomic/property characteristics (income, lot size, constructed area, household size, young children, literacy, electricity) and informal/coping water purchase prices plus monetized household hauling time. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, no eligibility rule, tenure/documentation requirement, regulated utility tariff or cost-recovery rule, administrative burden, enforcement practice, or utility ownership/regulatory structure governing service access is measured or analyzed; coping prices reflect unregulated vended/non-tap market prices and time costs of hauling.
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical econometric study analyzing 1995-1997 cross-sectional household survey data from 553 non-tap households in El Salvador and 826 non-tap households in Honduras using a two-step multinomial logit selection model (Lee correction) and OLS log-log demand regressions.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports household choice among non-tap coping water sources (private tap, public tap, private well, public well, tank trucks) and per household member monthly water consumption quantity (cubic meters per capita per month).
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (unconnected households in Santa Ana, Sonsonate, and San Miguel, El Salvador, and marginal barrios of Tegucigalpa, Honduras), exposures (total coping water cost = purchase price + monetized hauling time, household income, free-water savings, household/property characteristics), outcomes (coping water source selection and log monthly per-capita water consumption), and study design (cross-sectional observational survey econometrics) are all clearly specified.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is written in English.

study_design: Cross-sectional observational household survey econometric study (two-step multinomial logit selection model with Lee bias correction and OLS log-log demand estimation)
population_and_sample: Unconnected (non-tap) urban households surveyed in 1995-1997 in three cities in El Salvador (Santa Ana, Sonsonate, San Miguel; n = 553 total, 321 in multinomial logit and 312 in demand estimation) and in marginal barrios of Tegucigalpa, Honduras (n = 826 total, 733 in demand estimation); unit of analysis: household
exposure: Source-specific total coping water cost per cubic meter (informal/coping water purchase price plus monetized household hauling time cost), household income, money savings from free water access, and household/property characteristics (lot size, constructed area, household size, children under five, literacy, electricity availability)
outcome: Household selection among non-tap coping water sources (private tap, public tap, private well, public well, tank truck) and per household member monthly water consumption (cubic meters per capita per month)
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). Although this empirical household survey study examines non-tap coping water source selection and water consumption among unconnected urban households in El Salvador and Honduras (satisfying c1, c3, c4, c5, and c6), it models consumer price and income elasticities of non-tap water demand with respect to coping water purchase prices, monetized hauling time, household income, and demographic/property attributes. It does not measure or analyze any legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance mechanism (failing Criterion 2 under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading).
